{{Short description|Certain type of divisor of an integer}}
In [[mathematics]], a [[natural number]] {{mvar|a}} is a '''unitary divisor''' (or '''Hall divisor''') of a number {{mvar|b}} if {{mvar|a}} is a [[divisor]] of {{mvar|b}} and if {{mvar|a}} and {{mvar|b / a}} are [[coprime]], having no common factor other than 1. Equivalently, a divisor {{mvar|a}} of {{mvar|b}} is a unitary divisor [[if and only if]] every [[prime number|prime]] factor of {{mvar|a}} has the same [[multiplicity (mathematics)|multiplicity]] in {{mvar|a}} as it has in {{mvar|b}}.

The concept of a unitary divisor originates from [[Ramaswamy S. Vaidyanathaswamy|R. Vaidyanathaswamy]] (1931),<ref>{{cite journal |author=R. Vaidyanathaswamy |author-link=Ramaswamy S. Vaidyanathaswamy |title=The theory of multiplicative arithmetic functions |journal=Transactions of the American Mathematical Society |volume=33 |issue=2 |pages=579–662 |year=1931 |doi=10.1090/S0002-9947-1931-1501607-1|doi-access=free }}</ref> who used the term '''block divisor'''.

== Example ==

The integer 5 is a unitary divisor of 60, because 5 and <math>\frac{60}{5}=12</math> have only 1 as a common factor. 

On the contrary, 6 is a divisor but not a unitary divisor of 60, as 6 and <math>\frac{60}{6}=10</math> have a common factor other than 1, namely 2.

== Sum of unitary divisors ==

The sum-of-unitary-divisors function is denoted by the lowercase Greek letter sigma thus: <math>\sigma^*(n)</math>. The sum of the {{mvar|k}}-th [[exponentiation|powers]] of the unitary divisors is denoted by <math>\sigma_k^*(n)</math>:

:<math>\sigma_k^*(n) = \sum_{d \,\mid\, n \atop \gcd(d,\,n/d)=1} \!\! d^k.</math>

It is a [[multiplicative function]]. If the [[proper divisor|proper]] unitary divisors of a given number add up to that number, then that number is called a [[unitary perfect number]].

==Properties==
The number {{math|1}} is a unitary divisor of every natural number.

The number of unitary divisors of a number {{mvar|n}} is {{math|2{{sup|''k''}}}}, where {{mvar|k}} is the number of distinct prime factors of {{mvar|n}}. 
This is because each [[integer]] {{math|''N'' > 1}} is the product of positive powers <math>p^{r_p}</math> of distinct prime numbers {{mvar|p}}. Thus every unitary divisor of {{mvar|N}} is the product, over a given subset {{mvar|S}} of the prime divisors {{math|{''p''}}} of {{mvar|N}}, of the prime powers <math>p^{r_p}</math> for {{math|''p'' ∈ ''S''}}. If there are {{mvar|k}} prime factors, then there are exactly {{math|2{{sup|''k''}}}} subsets {{mvar|S}}, and the statement follows.

The sum of the unitary divisors of {{mvar|n}} is [[parity (mathematics)|odd]] if {{mvar|n}} is a [[power of 2]] (including {{math|1}}), and [[parity (mathematics)|even]] otherwise.

Both the count and the sum of the unitary divisors of {{mvar|n}} are [[multiplicative function]]s of {{mvar|n}} that are not [[completely multiplicative]]. The [[Dirichlet generating function]] is
:<math>\frac{\zeta(s)\zeta(s-k)}{\zeta(2s-k)} = \sum_{n\ge 1}\frac{\sigma_k^*(n)}{n^s}.</math>

Every divisor of {{mvar|n}} is unitary if and only if {{mvar|n}} is [[square-free integer|square-free]].

The set of all unitary divisors of {{mvar|n}} forms a [[Boolean algebra (structure)|Boolean algebra]] with meet given by the [[greatest common divisor]] and join by the [[least common multiple]]. Equivalently, the set of unitary divisors of {{mvar|n}} forms a Boolean ring, where the addition and multiplication are given by 
:<math>a\oplus b = \frac{ab}{(a,b)^2},\qquad a\odot b=(a,b)</math> 
where <math>(a,b)</math> denotes the greatest common divisor of {{mvar|a}} and {{mvar|b}}. <ref>{{cite journal |last1=Conway |first1=J.H. |last2=Norton |first2=S.P. |title=Monstrous Moonshine |journal=Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society |volume=11 |issue=3 |pages=308–339 |year=1979 |doi=10.1112/blms/11.3.308 | url= https://doi.org/10.1112/blms/11.3.308 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Odd unitary divisors ==
The sum of the ''k''-th powers of the odd unitary divisors is

:<math>\sigma_k^{(o)*}(n) = \sum_{{d \,\mid\, n \atop d \equiv 1 \pmod 2} \atop \gcd(d,n/d)=1} \!\! d^k.</math>

It is also multiplicative, with Dirichlet generating function

:<math>\frac{\zeta(s)\zeta(s-k)(1-2^{k-s})}{\zeta(2s-k)(1-2^{k-2s})} = \sum_{n\ge 1}\frac{\sigma_k^{(o)*}(n)}{n^s}.</math>

==Bi-unitary divisors==
A divisor {{mvar|d}} of {{mvar|n}} is a '''bi-unitary divisor''' if the greatest common unitary divisor of {{mvar|d}} and {{math|''n'' / ''d''}} is {{math|1}}.  This concept originates from D. Suryanarayana (1972). [The number of bi-unitary divisors of an integer, in The Theory of Arithmetic Functions, ''[[Lecture Notes in Mathematics]]'' 251: 273–282, New York, Springer–Verlag].

The number of bi-unitary divisors of {{mvar|n}} is a multiplicative function of {{mvar|n}} with [[Average order of an arithmetic function|average order]] <math>A \log x</math> where<ref name=Ivic395>Ivić (1985) p.395</ref>

:<math>A = \prod_p\left({1 - \frac{p-1}{p^2(p+1)} }\right) \ = 0.8073308216\cdots  . </math>

A '''bi-unitary perfect number''' is one equal to the sum of its bi-unitary aliquot divisors.  The only such numbers are {{math|6}}, {{math|60}} and {{math|90}}.<ref name=HNTI115>Sandor et al (2006) p.115</ref>

==[[OEIS]] sequences==
* {{OEIS2C|A034444}} is <math>\sigma^*_0(n)</math>
* {{OEIS2C|A034448}} is <math>\sigma^*_1(n)</math>
* {{OEIS2C|A034676}} to {{OEIS2C|A034682}} are <math>\sigma^*_2(n)</math> to <math>\sigma^*_8(n)</math>
* {{OEIS2C|A034444}} is <math>2^\omega(n)</math>, the number of unitary divisors
* {{OEIS2C|A068068}} is <math>\sigma^{(o)*}_0(n)</math>
* {{OEIS2C|A192066}} is <math>\sigma^{(o)*}_1(n)</math>
* {{OEIS2C|A064609}} is <math>\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma^*_{1}(i)</math>
* {{OEIS2C|A306071}} is the constant {{mvar|A}}
